**How the phase ends:** In this war Phase VI does not end with the fall of Saigon. On 31 December 1975 the Republic of Vietnam holds III and IV Corps, the coast from Nha Trang south and about half the population of 1974; the PAVN holds the Highlands, I Corps and the central coast north of Khanh Hoa, and five corps are assembled for an offensive on the capital in the first months of 1976 (EV011-3) [X-011]. That is a conclusion and not an assumption. The date of 30 April 1975 was set in Hanoi by a resolution to finish before the rains, and the resolution was made possible by the double collapse of I and II Corps in the second half of March; in this war Thieu's decision of 11–14 March went the other way, the Highlands were lost in a five-week siege instead of a ten-day rout, Hue in an ordered withdrawal on 18 April instead of a collapse on 25 March, and the Politburo, without a collapse to resolve on, put Saigon back to the dry season (EV000-94, EV000-95, EVMT01-4) [X-011]. The mechanism was political and at the top: a President in Washington who did not fall, an appropriation near the 1974 level, and a President in Saigon who believed, on that evidence, that he need not give anything up (F011-20, F011-21). It bought a season, and it was bought at a price. The refusal of the Dalat study cost the Republic half its Highland force and the 2nd Division, which a planned withdrawal in the dry season would have saved, and its reserve spent the spring at Da Nang, five hundred kilometres from the capital, until SOUTHERN WALL brought it home in May.

The Republic that enters 1976 is not the historical Republic, and it is not a Republic that has survived. Its fall is expected in the dry season of 1976, by my estimate between February and May, from an offensive on the capital by five corps that it has a rebuilt reserve, a full arsenal, its Delta and its capital's belt to meet, and no American air power (EV011-3) [X-011]. Rung (b) by the test of rules/RUNGS.toml, because Saigon stands past 30 April 1975; the outcome in its own terms is a reprieve of about a year, and the record ends before it is spent. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat into law and would not unwrite it for a President who asked; American military aid had fallen less than history's but had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment, and then chose to wait.

At the end of 1974, on the eve of Phuoc Long, the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region was held at night more firmly than history's, and the Front's district committees there had lost about twice the historical share of their members in 1973 (EV000-84) [X-006]; the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure was still the better for its ten years of files; the government's standing in the hamlets was history's, after the decrees of 1972; the army's battalions were better led and its divisions and corps no better; and the army as a whole was more dependent than history's on American fire it no longer had, and knew it (EV000-91, EV000-92) [X-MT01]. In this war the army had also fought 1974 near the 1973 allowance, with its aircraft flying and its relief columns fuelled, and lost perhaps 2,500–6,500 fewer men in the year than history's 30,000, a judgment on the two rates named in EV000-91 [X-008] [X-011]. At the end of 1975 the held belt and the files are still the Republic's, and the end vector measures a state that still exists.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the resolution of October 1975 that set the offensive on Saigon for 1976, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972 and the delay of 1975, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The timing of its campaign was its own, set by its army's road, the season and, in March 1975, by a map that did not offer it the collapse history had (EVMT01-4). The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead [H]. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans [H].

The squad guns and the marksmen's rifles of the ARVN's II Corps and of the 1st and 2nd Divisions are in the PAVN's hands by the end of the spring, with the hoards of Quang Ngai and the Highlands; the hoard at Hue was destroyed in place, and the hoards of III and IV Corps are still the Republic's [X-004] [X-011].

The Republic's defence of every besieged town had been built since 1971 around American bombers and American coordinates, and both were gone by the end of 1973 (EV000-86, EV000-92) [X-005]. At Pleiku in April 1975 it fought a siege without them, on fuel and rounds, and held three weeks (EV000-95).

The officers the reforms made fought 1975 as well as any part of the RVNAF fought it. Their best staff plan was refused in March and used in May, for SOUTHERN WALL and the rebuilding of the reserve (EV000-95, EV011-3). The board's files, with the evaluation report of every officer since 1964, are in the Joint General Staff's compound at the end of 1975 [X-007] [X-011].

The Republic's own plants stretched its aid dollar by about a third to two-fifths, kept its radios on the air through 1974, and in 1975 were the arsenal of an army that had lost its northern hoards; they shortened no collapse and lengthened none, because the spring of 1975 was decided by orders, families and an enemy who chose his ground, and at the end of the year they are still the Republic's (EV000-89, EVMT01-4, EV011-3) [X-008] [X-011].

# Card 013 — The air campaign against the North unrestricted: an opening strike on the full target list on 2 March 1965, and MACV targeting authority with standing restrike, no Hanoi or Haiphong zones, one strike on Haiphong's port, a 15-mile Chinese buffer and no pauses

*Memorandum 013 · status part2 · full record: memos/013/ · generated by fie.py*

## P013a · Opening strike of the air campaign against the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, 2 March 1965: a planned decapitating first blow on the 2026 model of the opening nights of DESERT STORM (17 January 1991) and IRAQI FREEDOM (March 2003), against the whole of the Joint Chiefs' target list in one compressed opening, planned by MACV and CINCPAC from the Gulf of Tonkin incident in August 1964, flown by the in-theater and carrier air forces with the B-52J, the GBU-31 and GBU-38 JDAM, the U-2S and the RQ-4B already in the record, against the command and control, air defence, airfields, power, fuel, transport and war industry of the North, with Haiphong's port infrastructure struck once and the port mined only in May 1972
one opening strike on the full target list, the JCS 94-target list of 1964 and its additions [U]; first strike on 2 March 1965 [U] · spaces none in RVN beyond the air units the record already holds; the strike is flown from Thailand, Guam, Okinawa and the carriers of TF 77 [E: basing of the 1965 air campaign] · arrives 1965-03-02 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · air

**Key figures.**
- Target list: the JCS Target Study of 94 targets, 24–27 August 1964, in five categories [M013·S1]; rejected by the White House historically [M013·S2]
- First strike 2 March 1965, planning from August 1964 [U]
- Threat on the day: about 1,500 AA guns (2,100 by another count), about 22 early-warning and 4 fire-control radars, about 36 MiG-17s, no SA-2 [M013·S5] [M013·S6] [M013·S3]
- Weight: 22–24 J sorties a day in the surge, about 440–480 GBU-31 a day [E: D5]; about 600–900 aimpoints on the list [E: D5]; the list struck in about three to four days [D]
- Kit stock on Guam, March 1965: about 8,000–12,000 GBU-31 and 15,000–25,000 GBU-38 [E: fourteen months of M005 deliveries]
- Tactical second wave: about 150–250 strike sorties on a flyable day [E: D5]
- History's benchmark: 180 aircraft lost to 24 December 1965 [M013·S6]; Hanoi and Haiphong targets from October–November 1965 [M013·S3]; Phuc Yen first struck 24 October 1967 [M013·S2]
- Within the year historically: more than 5,000 guns [M013·S6], 56 SAM sites [M013·S4]

**Negative specification.** The opening strike cannot decapitate the North. The Politburo, the Central Military Commission and the General Staff do not sit in the buildings on the list, and the Party commands the war in the South through COSVN, not through the Hanoi exchanges [E: the North's dispersed leadership]. It cannot stop the flow south: J-2 put the enemy's need from the North at 70–90 tons a day at the 1966 peak [M003], and a porter-and-bicycle Trail in 1965 does not depend on a power plant. It cannot strike Laos, where the ambassador keeps the targets, or close Haiphong, which is struck once and mined only in May 1972 [U]. It does not stop the third of the North's imports that come by rail from China [M013·S6], and the 15-mile buffer [U] leaves the last stretch of both rail lines untouched. The fighter-bombers of 1965 cannot bomb a point target at night or under the crachin of March [E: visual bombing in 1965], so on a bad week the strike is the Js' alone. It cannot prevent the Soviet SA-2 package (95 systems over the war [M013·S6]) or the Chinese support troops; it can only meet them earlier. And it does not change Washington's decision whether to bomb; it changes how much is struck once that decision is made.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the North the two and a half years of gradualism in which it built the world's densest air defence under sanctuary, from about 1,500 guns and no missiles in March 1965 to more than 5,000 guns within a year [M013·S6] and 56 SAM sites by December [M013·S4]. Phuc Yen's MiG-17s (about 36 aircraft [M013·S6]) are struck on the ground in the first hour, the four fire-control radars and about 22 warning radars [M013·S5] in the first night. It denies the North the use of its fixed infrastructure before it has learned to do without it: the power plants, the bulk fuel at Hanoi, Haiphong, Nam Dinh and Vinh, the Hanoi bridges and the rail yards, all at once and in any weather. And it denies Hanoi the reading of 1965 that the Americans would not dare: the North learns on the first night that the capital is not a sanctuary.

**Verdict.** The opening strike is the most efficient blow on the North's fixed targets that any American force in 1965 could deliver. The B-52J with about 1,400 GBU-31 in three days [D] does in the crachin of March what history's fighter-bombers did in two and a half years of weekly packages, and it catches an air defence of guns and MiG-17s before the first SA-2 arrives [M013·S3]. That buys a broken air defence for the first months of the campaign, fewer aircraft lost, and a North stripped of power, bulk fuel, bridges and airfields in a week. It does not buy the war. The North's war in the South in 1965 needs tens of tons a day [M003], carried by porters, bicycles and trucks that the list does not hold. Its leaders are not in the buildings, and its allies replace what is destroyed: Moscow ships the missiles faster and Beijing sends the engineers sooner. The strike is the end of gradualism and the start of a test the gradualists never made: whether a North that has lost everything that can be bombed will stop. History's answer, from 1972, is that it negotiates on its own timetable. The record's answer is for Parts 2 and 3.

## P013b · Standing authorities for the air campaign against the North, from 2 March 1965: COMUSMACV selects the targets north of the DMZ in place of Washington's weekly approval; standing permission to restrike any target; no restricted or prohibited zone around Hanoi or Haiphong; Haiphong's port infrastructure struck once only, everything else at and around Haiphong open; a 15-mile buffer along the Chinese border; no pauses or suspensions within the campaign; Washington keeps the decision whether to bomb at all; Laos targets stay with the ambassador; mining of the northern ports as historical, May 1972
one authority, held by COMUSMACV for the duration of the campaign [U]; buffer 15 miles [U] · spaces ~60–120 in an expanded MACV targeting and battle-damage cell at Tan Son Nhut [E: the Seventh Air Force and MACV J-2 targeting staffs of 1966–67] · arrives 1965-03-02 · STRIKE, INTERDICT · institutional

**Key figures.**
- Authority from 2 March 1965 [U]; COMUSMACV selects targets; standing restrike; no pauses [U]
- Buffer along China: 15 miles [U] against history's 30 miles west of 106° E and 25 east of it [M013·S2]
- Haiphong: port infrastructure struck once [U]; mined May 1972 [U]; two-thirds of the North's imports by sea, a third by rail from China [M013·S6]
- History's zones lifted: Hanoi restricted 30 miles, prohibited 10; Haiphong 10 and 4 [M013·S2]
- History's regime: 22 authorised fixed targets and 1,000 of 106,000 sorties against them in 1966 [M013·S2]; seven halts in three years and eight months [M013·S2]; Christmas halt 37 days [M013·S2]
- Targeting cell about 60–120 people at Tan Son Nhut [E: 1966–67 targeting staffs]; standing list about 200–400 targets, about 30–60 restrikes a week [E: D5]
- Soviet SA-2 deliveries over the war: 95 systems, 7,658 missiles [M013·S6]; 56 SAM sites by end 1965 historically [M013·S4]

**Negative specification.** The authority does not let me stop the bombing being stopped: the President keeps the decision whether to bomb, and the halt of 1 November 1968 stays his [U]. It does not let me close Haiphong. The port is struck once [U] and mined only in May 1972 [U], so two-thirds of the North's imports [M013·S6] keep arriving by sea, by lighter if not by crane. It does not let me strike within 15 miles of China [U], where the rail lines carry the other third [M013·S6]. It does not give me the Laos targets, which stay with the ambassador, or the Navy, whose carriers stay CINCPACFLT's and take my targets through CINCPAC. It does not make the North's fuel, stores and trucks fixed: after the first season they are dispersed under trees and in villages, as the record already shows from June 1966 (EVCP02-4). It does not measure itself honestly: the cell's battle-damage assessment is the claim of the organisation that chose the target (A13). And it does not make the North's war in the South depend on what can be bombed in the North.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the North its sanctuaries: Hanoi, the MiG bases, the SAM sites under construction, Haiphong's city and the 30-mile and 10-mile circles [M013·S2] in which history let it build, store and train. It denies the repair cycle its respite, because each repair is answered when the cell judges it done, not at the next weekly approval. It denies the pauses, the six days of May 1965 and the 37 days of Christmas 1965 [M013·S2], which the North used historically to repair, resupply and move forces south. And it denies Hanoi the reading that the war's escalation is a dial in Washington's hand that turns back whenever the President is pressed.

**Verdict.** The authority is the change the theater asked for throughout the war, and it buys what was asked for. A campaign against the North's fixed targets is fought as a campaign: targets chosen in the theater, struck when ready, restruck when repaired, without sanctuary and without pause. With the opening strike it makes the North's air defence a lesser and later threat, saves aircraft and crews, and keeps the bridges, power and rail of the North down for as long as Washington allows. It does not buy the end of the North's war in the South. Haiphong's cargo keeps coming by lighter after the port's one strike, and the Chinese rail keeps coming through the buffer. The Trail runs on porters, trucks and fords that the record has already shown no bombing stops. The halt that ends the campaign stays the President's, and removing the pauses spends his tolerance faster. The theater gets the campaign it wanted. The record will show whether that campaign was ever the war's decisive instrument, and history's 1972 suggests it was decisive only for the terms, not for the outcome.

## Employment concepts
EC013-1 the first night (Js from Guam, GPS kits) · EC013-2 the daylight wave (TF 77 and Thailand) · EC013-3 the restrike watch · EC013-4 the missile sites before the missiles · EC013-5 Haiphong's one strike, opening night · EC013-6 the rail war at the buffer's edge. Abandoned: EC013-7 decapitation (no instrument fixes a person in a city) · EC013-8 the dikes (no effect on the South; China; ends the campaign) · EC013-9 daylight armed reconnaissance of the roads, in part (trucks move at night)

## Interactions
- P013a, P013b × P005a, P005b, P005c: the J with GPS kits flies the opening night in the crachin and restrikes the bridges and power plants at the cell's tempo; the authority turns memorandum 005's bridge night into a campaign (F013-1)
- P013a, P013b × P003a, P003b: the U-2S's change detection and the Gulf watch see each repair, each SAM site under construction and each lighter out of Haiphong; restrike is ordered on measured evidence, and battle-damage assessment has a second ledger (F013-1, F013-16)
- P013b × P005d: the river and estuary fields south of the 20th parallel (EV005-3) and the restruck rail and road north of it squeeze the panhandle's freight from both ends; Haiphong itself stays unmined until May 1972 (F013-5)
- P013b × P003b (Sihanoukville count): pressure on the northern routes shows up as more Chinese-flag cargo counted at Kompong Som (F013-6)
- P013a × P012a: the combined command's planning staff gives the VNAF's A-1 squadrons their place in the opening strike on the coastal targets; nothing else in the combined command touches the North (F013-4)


## Standing directives

- **DIRCP01-1** · In each Part 3, take at least one causal chain from an earlier memorandum whose later links fall in a phase this memorandum revises, and test it against the war as now written; where the new provision or free play makes it resolve differently, say so in the chain review and let it (every chain in memoranda 001–005 resolved as predicted, which is more likely tidiness than foresight)
- **DIRCP01-2** · A war-wide figure for lives saved, or any war-wide count built from a rate, must be shown at work in at least two dated events in the chapters before a later memorandum repeats it; until then it is cited as a judgment resting on its rate, with the rate named (CP01 calibration of the [X-004] lives-saved figure)
- **DIRMT01-1** · In every §4.N, state the date of the Republic's fall as its own estimate, separately from the rung: a window, the mechanisms in the cumulative force that pull it earlier and those that pull it later, and which dominate and why; "on the historical timeline" may be written only as the conclusion of that test, and a change of date is reported as a change of date and does not by itself move the rung between (a) and (b) while the ladder's overlap stands (the historical fall, twenty-five months after the last American combat troops left, satisfies the words of rung (b), and seven memoranda have kept (a) and (b) apart by the date alone)
- **DIRMT01-2** · In every §4.N, carry a running sum of the sub-band estimates that all memoranda so far have made on the same variable (American dead, ARVN battalions not lost, and the like), tagged as exercise judgments with their rates named, and say whether the sum crosses a band; and treat the American aid appropriation of 1974 and the refusal of April 1975 as events a provision can change, not as history to be carried (each memorandum judged its own saving of American lives alone, and the 1974 vote was never examined)
- **DIRMT01-3** · Where a chapter's end vector returns a variable to the historical state from a non-zero band in the phase before, the chapter must contain the dated events that produce the convergence; and in every memorandum that revises Phase VI, state in the phase's analysis the Republic's state at the end of 1974, before the last offensive, because the phase's end vector is measured after the fall and cannot record anything the fall erased (Phase V returned four countryside variables to history with no sentence on the countryside, and Phase VI's vector is blind by construction)
- **DIRMT01-4** · Where a memorandum alters an event and keeps its historical outcome, name what absorbs the difference (the enemy's choice to bypass or decline, a decision above the level the provision reached, an external fixed by law or by another government) and show it in the event; "as historically" is a conclusion, never a mechanism (in Phase VI at least six altered events in the last campaign restore the historical outcome by statement)
- **DIRMT01-5** · Where a perverse effect or a capture undoes a gain, state the net in both directions with its weight, and where several provisions' institutions fall to the same mechanism in the same years, judge them together before judging each alone (four institutions from four memoranda fall to the lapse of the American lever in 1970–71, each judged alone, and every memorandum closes on the gain undone)
- **DIRMT01-6** · The next memorandum or review whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI states the PAVN's 1972 losses in this war against the historical figure and the rebuilding time that follows, before writing 1973–75 (memorandum 005 made the measured sieges the enemy's worst battles; Phase V keeps the historical losses and Phase VI the historical rebuilding)
- **DIRMT01-7** · Every memorandum whose Part 3 revises Phase V or VI tests its effects against the critical path of 1975 (the palace's orders of 13–14 March, the 1st Corps' march against the rains, and Minh's surrender) and states whether any mechanism could delay the collapse of I and II Corps by about three weeks, the threshold beyond which the assault falls into the rains; effects on fights the PAVN could bypass are reported as such (the date of the fall was carried for seven memoranda without its critical path ever being stated)
- **DIRMT01-8** · Every memorandum touching the countryside states its effect separately for the Delta, the coastal lowlands of I and II Corps, the Highlands and their peoples, and the Saigon belt, and names a place in each where the effect is shown or says why there is none (the Delta was written as a footnote, the Montagnards appear twice and FULRO never, and Binh Dinh vanished from the record after 1967)
- **DIRMT01-9** · Every provision touching the reliability of the ARVN or the territorial forces addresses the soldier's family: where it lives, what his pay buys after inflation, and what happens to it when the unit moves or the front gives way (the corps of 1975 dissolved toward their families, and no memorandum had treated them)
- **DIRMT01-10** · The enemy's decisions have authors: in each memorandum name the body or commander who took the enemy's decision of G3, and distinguish Hanoi, the B-2 Front and COSVN, and the regional fronts where they differed; treat the Soviet and Chinese supply as variables with their own politics (COSVN vanishes from the record after 1971, the Phuoc Long argument is told as one mind, and the Soviet deliveries of 1974 are absent)
- **DIRMT01-11** · Every memorandum touching the countryside or the RVNAF states its effect on rice (production, procurement and the Front's take) and on the piaster and the soldier's pay, with at least one dated event (rice appears eleven times in Phase II and once in 1972–75, the years the economy decided)
- **DIRCP02-1** · At each checkpoint, consolidate a chapter over the limit in two steps: first merge minor historical events into summary events, then merge each memorandum's own minor NEW events in that phase into one summary per memorandum, keeping every fact a later memorandum or position cites by event number; and every memorandum's §4 adds to a phase's overview and ending only one paragraph, replacing rather than appending where an earlier memorandum's paragraph states the same variable (CP02 consolidation of P1 and P2, still about 7,600 and 9,300 words over the limit after the first step)
- **DIRCP02-2** · In each Part 3 the chain taken under DIRCP01-1 must be one written by another memorandum whose terminal event this memorandum did not write; C006-4, whose terminal link no chapter carries, is the first such chain for any memorandum revising Phase V (17 of 19 chains in memoranda 006–010 resolved as their authors predicted)
- **DIRCP02-3** · Where a provision acts on a variable already at the cap of the bands in a phase, the memorandum states its increment in the running sum of DIRMT01-2 with the factors it multiplies and how they overlap, and names the target the enemy moves to in answer (POSCP02-2); a product of overlapping judgments is reported as a range with its upper bound marked (CP02 calibration of the battalions-not-broken figure)
- **DIRR01-1** · DIRCP02-3's rule for a variable "already at the cap of the bands" lapses, because the scale has no cap short of a different war: a provision that acts on such a variable re-judges its range, and the range of the facet it acts on, and the running sums of DIRMT01-2 now say which part of that range they support rather than whether they cross a band; the rest of DIRCP02-3 stands, the target the enemy moves to in answer is still named, and a product of overlapping judgments is still reported as a range with its upper bound marked (the user's change of scale, 24 Nov 2026; R01)
- **DIRR01-2** · A range marked "converted" is the old band restated, not a judgment: it is never cited as a judgment of the war, and every memorandum or checkpoint whose evidence bears on a converted entry, or on one of the four entries converted from the cap, re-judges it with a confidence and a note (R01's mechanical conversion of the end vectors)
- **DIRR01-3** · Where a variable has facets, §2 names the facet a provision acts on, and every revised phase that judges a facet names the parent's binding facet and says why it binds; the parent is never the average of its facets, and a gain on one facet is not reported as a gain on the parent unless the binding facet moved (the user's point of 24 Nov 2026 that "ARVN effectiveness" does not discriminate between urban combat, combined arms, anti-armor and the rest)
- **DIRR02-1** · A study describes the war and never changes it: no study adds, alters or cancels an event or moves the end state, and where a study finds the record inconsistent it records a question for an erratum or a checkpoint rather than settling it (the user's design of 24 Nov 2026; R02)
- **DIRR02-2** · Every memorandum whose variables a study covers is written against that study: Part 2 judges its pushes against the study's values and says plainly when the provision's effect contradicts the study and which should give way, and Part 3 records what changed in the area in the study's entry (R02)
- **DIRR02-3** · A study's value is never cited as a measurement: study values are exercise judgments on the R01 scale, an indicator a study gives carries its own provenance, and a figure the study generates carries the X-tag of its study run (X-ST01 and so on) forever (A13a; R02)

## Settled positions on this memorandum's variables

- **POSTNA-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, ENEMY.regeneration, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia · While the enemy controls whether to accept battle and regenerates in sanctuary, attrition has no crossover point; a strategy that waits for one waits for something the geometry does not permit (TNA G-8)
- **POSTNA-4** · vars: TRAIL.capacity, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · On the opening date the enemy's external requirement from the North is of the order of 20 tons a day against a Trail of 20–30 tons a day and an uncounted sea route; Trail capacity is elastic with labour, so interdiction is judged only by tonnage arriving below the requirement, never by trucks or porters destroyed (TNA G-9)
- **POSTNA-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap, US.casualties · The American political clock is spent by casualties, cost and time, and fastest by the discovery that reported progress was false; a provision that improves a metric without improving the war shortens the clock (TNA G-5, G-10)
- **POS001-3** · vars: HANOI.will · Reform that erodes the Front's base raises Hanoi's urgency and shifts the arguments inside the Politburo; it does not change Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification or the timing of its decisions to invade (001 §2 F001-12; §4.P2)
- **POS003-1** · vars: FIND.main_force, FIX.capability, STRIKE.responsiveness · Airborne radar and signals reconnaissance find the enemy's movement in the open and his headquarters' transmitters, never his regiments under canopy; their value in any engagement equals what can be put on a track within the hour, and an improvement in finding is never claimed as an improvement in fixing (003 §2 F003-5; §4.P2–P5)
- **POS003-2** · vars: INFIL.sea, SANCT.cambodia, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · In this war the sea route to the South's coast closed in 1964 under observation and the enemy's southern supply moved to Sihanoukville from June 1965; supply through Cambodia, not by sea, is the principal external line into III and IV Corps from 1965 until Lon Nol's coup (003 §2 F003-3; EV003-2)
- **POS003-3** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap · In this war no attack of 4 August 1964 was claimed and Pierce Arrow was not flown; the Southeast Asia Resolution rests on the attack of 2 August, and the Tonkin deception is not part of the credibility gap in any later phase (003 §4.P1, §4.P3; EV000-3)
- **POS004-2** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance · In this war the ARVN and the RF/PF carry modern carbines from 1964, and the 1967 M16 crisis and inquiry and the 1968–69 rearmament do not occur; from 1969 the historical army has caught up, and the remaining difference is the squad gun, the marksman and the practice (004 F004-6; §4.P2–P4)
- **POS005-1** · vars: STRIKE.responsiveness, FIND.main_force, FIX.capability · GPS weapons change what dies at a measured coordinate, never what can be located; in this war the J's precision is decisive where the enemy holds still long enough to be measured, at the siege and the fixed crossing, and adds nothing against the main force under canopy or the infrastructure in the hamlets (005 §2 F005-1, F005-7, F005-21)
- **POS005-2** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, FIX.capability, US.political_tolerance · In this war the defence of besieged positions from 1965 rests on the B-52J and an American coordinate cell; it is far stronger while American air power is present and leaves the RVNAF more dependent on it when it goes (005 §2 F005-20)
- **POS005-4** · vars: TRAIL.capacity, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · In this war the panhandle's fixed crossings were cut by the B-52J from April 1966, and Group 559 rebuilt the net as braided fords, causeways and pontoons with no single point of failure; from 1966 the Trail is more redundant than history's, and precision strikes on crossings are never counted as reductions in tonnage arriving (005 §4.P2; EV005-2, EV000-55)
- **POSCP01-1** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.credibility_gap · The small gains on the American clock in memoranda 001–005 (no Tonkin deception, honest damage assessment, no M16 scandal, a conviction in 1967, fewer prisoners and no Bach Mai in 1972) narrow the credibility gap and do not move tolerance by a band in any phase, because the clock was spent by the casualties of 1965–68 and by Tet, which no provision changed and one made sharper (CP01 §3; C003-3)
- **REVMT01-1** · reverses POS001-3 · vars: HANOI.will, ENEMY.engagement_control, PAVN.strength_south · Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification is fixed throughout and nothing in the force reaches it (G-14); the timing of its offensives is not fixed, and the schedule of the last campaign in particular was set week by week by the ARVN's behaviour in 1975 (the plan for 1976 accelerated after Phuoc Long and again after the Highlands, EV000-92); a memorandum that changes the ARVN, the PAVN's losses or the Republic's state on the eve of the offensive must test what it does to that schedule (MT01 M-6, M-10, M-12)
- **POSMT01-2** · vars: PAVN.strength_south, ENEMY.regeneration · In this war the PAVN's killed and wounded in 1972 were about a tenth above the historical figure, concentrated in the 5th, 7th, 9th, 320th and 2nd Divisions at An Loc and Kontum; the North replaced the men within its 1973 flow and formed its corps on the historical dates, so the extra loss cost the 1974–75 divisions quality and not time (MT01 M-1; EV000-87)
- **POSMT01-3** · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The date of the Republic's fall, 30 April 1975 within a window of about 27 April to the first days of May, is derived and not carried: it was set by Hanoi's resolution of 25 March to finish before the rains and by the 1st Corps' march, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps would have moved it, by putting the assault into the rains; better ARVN units act on fights the PAVN bypasses and do not reach that threshold (MT01 M-12; EVMT01-4, EV000-96)
- **POSMT01-5** · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.casualties, US.credibility_gap · The sum of the American lives the provisions saved is a judgment of about 2,500–5,000, mostly in 1965–69, five to nine percent of the historical dead, below a band; it does not move tolerance, and the changes in the record that bear on the 1974 appropriation roughly cancel, so the vote stands as history's until a provision changes what the Republic needs Congress to pay for (MT01 M-7; EV000-89)
- **POS008-1** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, ADVISE.leverage, US.political_tolerance · A domestic arsenal, battery works and rebuild depot stretch the aid dollar in 1974–75 only if the RVNAF has been made to buy from them while American supply was free; this headquarters adopts a domestic share enforced by the Aid Compliance Board from 1965, and the stretch changes what the fiscal 1975 appropriation buys, not the vote (008 §2 F008-2, F008-20, F008-23)
- **POS008-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · A radio kept on the air at the post supplies the means of calling help in POSTNA-2 and moves the post's binding constraint to the reaction and fire within range; the Front answers by attacking the relief and the posts that cannot call, and the radio's gain appears as attacks not made (008 §2 F008-1, F008-3, F008-6, F008-16)
- **POS008-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, US.political_tolerance, HANOI.will · In this war the Republic's own arsenal and battery works stretched the fiscal 1975 appropriation to about $850 million–$1 billion of history's and kept its ammunition and communications from going dark in 1974, but delayed the collapse of I and II Corps by days, not the three weeks that would have moved the date; domestic sustainment without an air arm the Republic owns and a choice of corps commanders does not move the rung (008 §4.P6, §4.N; EV000-89, EVMT01-4)
- **POS008-4** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness · From 1967 the territorial post's first call is for fire, not men, after the Front's ambush of the relief at My Phuoc Tay; this makes the post cheaper to hold and keeps the platoon behind its wire, so that the post is held better and the hamlet outside it is not, and the call passes to Vietnamese district guns in 1970–71 (008 §4.P2, §4.P4; EV008-4, EV008-7)
- **POS009-2** · vars: MED.survival, US.casualties, US.political_tolerance · In this war every soldier of both armies is taught the tourniquet in basic training; the saving is a judgment on a rate of two to four percent of killed in action, shown at Albany and in the first wave of Tet, about 900–1,900 Americans and 4,000–12,000 South Vietnamese, below a band on every variable and proof against enemy adaptation (009 §4.P2, §4.P3, §4.N; EV000-23, EV000-42)
- **POS010-4** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, STRIKE.responsiveness · The American NCO course carries the habit of fixing the enemy and calling fire down to the ARVN squad; it is a strength the Republic owns only where the gun at the other end is Vietnamese, as at Long My, and a dependence everywhere else (010 F010-24; EV008-7)
- **POS011-1** · vars: US.political_tolerance, NEGOT.position · In this war there is no Watergate: Nixon serves to January 1977, the Senate hearings, the Saturday Night Massacre, impeachment and resignation never happen, and the War Powers override fails; Case–Church still passes in June 1973 by veto-proof margins, so the end of American combat in Indochina on 15 August 1973 is law, and the binding constraint on American support from 1973 is Congress, not the President (011 F011-7, F011-9; EV000-86)
- **POS011-2** · vars: US.political_tolerance, ARVN.self_sufficiency · American military aid to the RVNAF is about $950 million for fiscal 1975, buying through the domestic stretch about what $1.2 billion bought historically, with supplementals of about $150 million in March and $175 million in May 1975 and about $800 million for fiscal 1976; the money reached fuel, aircraft and heavy rounds and saved perhaps 1,500–4,000 of the Republic's dead in 1974, and it never reached the soldier's pay or the artillery duel with the 130mm (011 F011-2, F011-21; EV000-89, EV000-91, EV011-2, EV000-97, EV011-3)
- **POS011-5** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.political_tolerance, US.casualties · A quarter of the historically inducted enlisted voluntarily in the same jobs (Reading A); draft calls are a quarter smaller and the force is unchanged; the volunteers die at the draftees' rate and are about half as likely to be on the drug and refusal lists of 1970–71, with no change to any battle (011 F011-15, F011-19; EV010-5)
- **REV011-1** · reverses POSMT01-3 · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The method of POSMT01-3 stands: the date of the fall is derived from Hanoi's calendar, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps moves it. What is reversed is the date. In this war the collapse came three to five weeks late, because Thieu gave no withdrawal order on 13–14 March 1975; the Politburo put the assault on Saigon back to the dry season of 1975–76, and the fall is expected between February and May 1976 (011; EVMT01-4, EV000-94, EV000-95)
- **REV011-2** · reverses POSMT01-5 · vars: US.political_tolerance, US.casualties, US.credibility_gap · The sum of the American lives saved stands at about 3,700–7,800 and does not move tolerance. What is reversed is the vote: the fiscal 1975 appropriation is no longer history's, because the President who fought for it was not fighting impeachment, and the April 1975 request is Nixon's and partly voted (011 F011-17; EV000-89, EV000-97)

- **Truong Vinh Khoa** · Commissioner Against Corruption from 1 January 1964, formerly a judge of the Saigon Court of Appeal · invented in 001 · Refused to charge the Dalat generals without evidence, convicted the Sa Dec ammunition ring in 1967 on cartridge lot numbers and a general the same year, audited Phoenix from 1968, kept in office but placed under the presidential Inspectorate in 1971
- **Phan Duy Khiem** · Brigadier General, IV Corps deputy commander for logistics 1965–67 · invented in 001 · Convicted by the Special Court on 18 April 1967 of ration and fuel diversion and sentenced to eight years
- **Vo Dinh Cuong** · Director General of National Police 1 January 1964 – 12 March 1966, formerly an inspector of the Sûreté · invented in 002 · Detained in Khanh's coup and restored in three days, kept the police out of the September 1964 coup, removed by Ky's decree in March 1966 and replaced by Loan
- **Dinh Quang Tuyen** · Judge of the Court of Cassation, chairman of the Provincial Administration Selection Board from 1 January 1964 · invented in 002 · Published the first list on 27 April 1964; the Board he chaired outlived four governments and was packed by Thieu in 1970
- **Ha Thuc Lan** · Lieutenant Colonel, engineer officer, province chief of Long An from June 1964 · invented in 002 · Placed third in the first examination; planned Operation NIGHT LANTERN with the rule that no post was settled without its platoon and a reaction within the hour
- **Le Cong Phuong** · Major, district chief of Can Giuoc from 1964, a native of Can Duoc · invented in 002 · Co-planned NIGHT LANTERN and returned the 1964 titles to their families in April 1966
- **Tran Van Sang** · Major, district chief of Mo Cay, Kien Hoa, June 1964 – November 1965 · invented in 002 · Killed by a command-detonated mine on 14 November 1965, the Front's "most harmful" district chief in the province
- **Harold Kessling** · Major, later Lieutenant Colonel, USAF; chief of the radar and imagery exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut from 1964 · invented in 003 · Had the watch on the night of 4 August 1964 and reported no boats near the destroyers; built the Sihanoukville count night by night from 1965 to the joint estimate of March 1967
- **Arthur L. Venn** · Lieutenant Colonel, US Army; chief of the MACV small-arms new-equipment training team from January 1964 · invented in 004 · Ran Operation IRON GATE under the rule that no new weapon left a depot until the old one came in and no carbine went to a post unzeroed; refused to shorten the course for the corps commanders
- **Lam Van Thien** · Lieutenant Colonel, province chief of Chuong Thien in 1966 · invented in 004 · Protested in writing the corps' borrowing of his Regional Force companies in April 1966; his returns of the posts lost became the case for the 1967 rule that RF companies belong to their province
- **Edwin T. Sorrell** · Major, later Lieutenant Colonel, USAF; chief of the coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut from March 1964 to its disbandment in September 1973, formerly a geodesist of the Aeronautical Chart and Information Center · invented in 005 · Found the map datum error and ruled that no map coordinate would be given to a guided bomb; built the folders of 1964–65 and ran the siege box at Con Thien, Khe Sanh, Lam Son 719, An Loc and Kontum
- **Tran Dinh Hieu** · Lieutenant Colonel, later Colonel, Military Security; director of the national Phung Hoang centre 1 January 1964 – February 1970 · invented in 006 · Kept the centres behind the posts and refused them to provinces without night security; withdrew the raid files after Duc Thanh; resigned when the palace moved the file in 1970
- **Martin J. Ashby** · Lieutenant Colonel, US Army; chief of the American Phung Hoang cell and exploitation detachment from 1964 · invented in 006 · Built the charts of the district committees from every arrest and rallier; supported Hieu's refusal of centres to the contested provinces
- **Samuel J. Whitcomb** · Captain, US Army, Selected Advisory Corps; subsector adviser of Can Giuoc October 1964 – April 1966 · invented in 006 · Served through the aftermath of the killings and NIGHT LANTERN; his report of April 1966 said the committee's arrest, not the sweep, broke the tax
- **Ngo Van Tam** · Captain, Special Branch; chief of the Hoc Mon DIOCC from July 1964 · invented in 006 · Planned Operation STILL WATER, which broke the Hoc Mon district committee in 1965
- **Carl E. Haney** · Major, US Army, Selected Advisory Corps; subsector adviser of Dien Ban, Quang Nam, 1965–67 · invented in 006 · Walked the relieving Marine companies over their ground in August 1966 and gave them the PF leaders who reported the R-20's withdrawal
- **Walter K. Dorsey** · Lieutenant Colonel, USMC; commanding officer, 1st Battalion, 26th Marines, 1965–67 · invented in 006 · Brought the battalion to Dien Ban as a unit; held the breach at La Huan in August 1966; reported in August 1967 that his Marines "do everything right in a firefight and are given none" after a year in which mines killed two-thirds of his dead
- **Phan Khac Minh** · Brigadier General; chairman of the Officer Selection and Promotion Board from 1 January 1964, formerly head of the General Staff's personnel directorate 1955–57 · invented in 007 · Sent to a training camp by Diem for refusing to promote the Can Lao's men; struck the bargain with Khanh in February 1964 that confirmed eleven of twenty-three coup promotions and refused twelve
- **Robert E. Lindqvist** · Colonel, US Army; chief of the American advisory cell to the Officer Selection Board from 1964 · invented in 007 · Built the evaluation system's trainers' course at Fort Benning; estimated in 1966 that half the sale of commands had ended and half had changed its name
- **Bui Quang Trieu** · ARVN officer commissioned from Thu Duc in 1957; major commanding 2nd Battalion, 9th Regiment, 5th Division from 1965; colonel commanding a 5th Division regiment from 1968 and the 3rd Division's 57th Regiment from 1971; Dalat faculty from 1972 · invented in 007 · Walked his flanks on Route 13 on 4 May 1966 and the 272nd declined its ambush; refused to sign the colonels' petition; held the Thach Han bridges at Quang Tri on 1 May 1972; led the Dalat seminar that wrote the reduced-resources study of November 1974
- **Dang Huu Thoi** · Lieutenant Colonel, commander of the VC 272nd Regiment in 1966 · invented in 007 · Withdrew the regiment from its ambush in the Xa Cam rubber on 4 May 1966 without firing, and ambushed an RF convoy at Bau Bang on 21 May
- **Vu Ngoc Hoan** · Colonel, commander of the ARVN 25th Division from March 1967 · invented in 007 · The list's second name; moved the dependents' quarters inside the perimeters and paid the ration in rice after the devaluation of 1966, cutting the division's desertion by about a quarter
- **Truong Cong Hy** · Lieutenant, clerk of the Officer Selection Board's secretariat 1965–67 · invented in 007 · Copied every command list for the B2 Front's military intelligence; arrested on 11 October 1967
- **Nguyen Dac Khiet** · Colonel, commanding a regiment of the 9th Division in 1970 · invented in 007 · Drafted the colonels' petition of September 1970 for the restoration of the general-officer list; moved to the Dalat faculty in the purge of December 1970
- **Van Tien Dung** · General, PAVN Chief of the General Staff · HIST · In this war argued on 31 March 1975 against an assault into the rains and set the offensive on Saigon for 1976
- **Hoang Cam** · Major General, commander of the PAVN 4th Corps 1974–75 · HIST · Took Phuoc Long in December 1974; at Xuan Loc stopped assaulting the 18th Division after three days and cut the town off, so that its twelve days were his schedule, not the defence's
- **Tran Van Tra** · Lieutenant General, commander of the B-2 Front · HIST · In this war won the argument for Phuoc Long against a more cautious Politburo, and lost the argument of 31 March 1975 for a thrust on Saigon in May
- **Nguyen Khoa Nam** · Major General, commander of IV Corps 1974–75 · HIST · Held IV Corps whole to 30 April, obeyed Minh's order to lay down arms, and took his own life on 1 May 1975
- **Ly Tong Ba** · Brigadier General, commander of the 23rd Division at Kontum in 1972 and the 25th Division in 1975 · HIST · Held Kontum in 1972; held Cu Chi and Route 1 west of Saigon in April 1975 until the 3rd Corps came on him, and was captured
- **Pham Van Phu** · Major General, commander of II Corps 1974–75 · HIST · In this war ordered to hold, gave up Kontum on 27 March 1975, held Pleiku three weeks and broke out down Route 19 on 14 April with the families at the head of the column
- **Huynh Cong Tri** · Major, district chief of Long My, Chuong Thien, from 1966, a list chief · invented in MT01 · Took the call for fire into Vietnamese hands with the district's gun platoon in 1970–71; kept all forty-one of his posts through the offensive of 1972 and lost the road to Vi Thanh for seven weeks
- **Dao Van Luong** · Major, district chief of Hoai Nhon, Binh Dinh, from 1966 · invented in MT01 · Burned the Bong Son Special Branch files on 22 April 1972, three hours before the town fell to the PAVN 3rd Division
- **Vuong Dinh Toan** · Director of Defence Industry 1 January 1964 – February 1970, a metallurgist trained at the École Centrale who built the Bien Hoa melt shop · invented in 008 · Ran the Directorate through the domestic share, the Da Nhim towers and the Phu Cat lot; replaced by a general of the President's staff in February 1970
- **Howard B. Teague** · Colonel, US Army Ordnance Corps; chief of the advisory element to the Directorate of Defence Industry from 1964 · invented in 008 · Proposed in November 1964 the domestic share that the Aid Compliance Board adopted on 1 March 1965
- **Le Van Muoi** · Sergeant, commander of the PF platoon at the Ap My Loi post, My Phuoc Tay, Cai Lay, Dinh Tuong · invented in 008 · Called the district on the night of 9 March 1967; his post held every attack for the rest of the war
- **Nguyen Thanh Liem** · Major, district chief of Cai Lay, Dinh Tuong, from 1965, a list chief · invented in 008 · Sent the 247th RF Company up the canal road on 9 March 1967 and lost 31 men at the culvert; wrote the rule that a post's first call is for fire and reliefs move by water or at dawn
- **Vu Xuan Dac** · Brigadier General, of the President's military staff; Director of Defence Industry from February 1970 · invented in 008 · Took the Directorate's contracts, licences and deferment list into the palace's gift; left Saigon on 28 April 1975
- **Daniel R. Kearsley** · Major, US Army, Selected Advisory Corps; subsector adviser of Long My, Chuong Thien, 1969–71 · invented in 008 · Handed the call for fire to the district's territorial gun platoon in 1970–71 and listened without speaking
- **Le Duan** · First Secretary of the Workers' Party of Vietnam · HIST · In this war cut back the autumn raids of 1974 and on 25–31 March 1975 put the offensive on Saigon back to the dry season of 1975–76
- **Tran Van Hai** · Sergeant Major, senior drill sergeant of the drill-sergeant academy at the Quang Trung Training Center from 1957, a member of its first class · invented in 009 · Trained the drill sergeants of the ten-week course and kept the rule that a recruit takes his orders from a Vietnamese
- **Raymond F. Coyle** · Lieutenant Colonel, US Army; chief of the MACV advisory detachment to the Central Training Command 1964–67 · invented in 009 · Watched and scored the centres and did not teach; backed the refusal of June 1964 to return a third of the drill sergeants to the battalions
- **Pham Van Tho** · Corporal, PF platoon at the Long Huu post, Kien Hoa, trained at the Ben Tre centre in 1962 · invented in 009 · Kept a third of the platoon's ammunition for the second assault on 17 November 1964 and brought his two wounded alive to the Ham Long boats
- **Lam Quang Phuc** · Master Sergeant First Class, senior instructor of the National NCO Academy at Dong De from 1957, a Tonkinese who came south with the Commando School in 1954 · invented in 010 · Taught every class from 1957; kept the academy's course whole through the mobilization and the National Day decree of 1970
- **William H. Rourke** · Master Sergeant, US Army; senior NCO adviser to the Dong De academy from 1963, a Korean War platoon sergeant · invented in 010 · Advised the Vietnamese faculty rather than teaching; his successor left in March 1971 and reported the course taught as he had found it
- **Nguyen Van Thuoc** · Master Sergeant, first sergeant of the 2nd Company, 4th Vietnamese Marine Battalion, in 1964 · invented in 010 · Took the company when its captain fell at Binh Gia on 31 December 1964 and brought it back to the perimeter by bounds
- **Tran Van Loc** · Sergeant First Class, later Master Sergeant, senior platoon sergeant of a company of the 3rd Battalion, 11th Regiment, 7th Division · invented in 010 · Held the company at Hau My on 16 November 1966 after its officers fell and called the Cai Be battery onto the tree line in eleven minutes
- **Nguyen Huu Tam** · Captain, commanding a company of the 3rd Battalion, 11th Regiment, 7th Division, in 1966 · invented in 010 · Wounded in the first minutes of the ambush at Hau My; returned to the battalion in March 1967

- **Phan Van Huong** · Brigadier General, chief of the Central Training Command in 1970–71 · invented in 010 · Ruled on 20 November 1970 that no man promoted by the National Day decree could rise again without his course

- **Nguyen Van Thieu** · President of the Republic of Vietnam · HIST · Refused the Dalat study on 11 March 1975 and gave no withdrawal order on 13–14 March; did not resign; took the study's method for SOUTHERN WALL in May 1975

- **Cao Van Vien** · General, Chief of the Joint General Staff · HIST · Presented the Dalat study to Thieu on 11 March 1975 and sent it back on 6 May as a plan for the defence of Saigon

Garvin** · Major, US Army Special Forces, commander of the task force's III Corps task group 1964–66 · invented in 012 · Ran DRY SEASON, which found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section, and FOLLOW THROUGH, which took the region finance section's ledger at Phu Hoa Dong
- **Nguyen Huu Phuoc** · Captain, then Lieutenant Colonel, Police Special Branch, deputy of the III Corps task group 1964–66 · invented in 012 · Received Ba Lien at Tan An at 0710 on 6 October 1964; held the Special Branch's veto over the task group's raids
- **Harold J. Beck** · Lieutenant Colonel, US Army, commander of the task force's II Corps task group 1965–66 · invented in 012 · Adopted the 64-name list on the II Corps coast, which killed a family at Hoa Thanh and was ended on 2 April 1966
- **Nguyen Van Tu** · Secretary of the Hoc Mon district committee · invented in 012 · Escaped STILL WATER and FOLLOW THROUGH and governed Hoc Mon from the Ho Bo woods from January 1966

## Trajectory Log — last 5 entries

## Memo 009 — Basic training to the 2026 standard for every US and RVNAF enlisted entrant from 1957, with an abridged course for the Regional and Popular Forces

Memorandum 009 trained every private soldier of both armies from 1957, the Americans to their services' 2026 courses, the ARVN to a ten-week course on the same programme and the territorials to six weeks of it, and found that training changes who lives, not who wins. Every soldier carried the tourniquet drill, and about 5,000–14,000 men lived who had died historically, at Thuan Loi, at Albany and in the streets at Tet. The trained post held its first ten minutes nineteen times in twenty; the trained battalion was attacked less, so its gain was invisible. The enemy answered by moving his war to the mine in Quang Nam, to the sapper, and to the self-defence hamlets of 1968, and the devaluation of 1966 sent trained deserters home and some to the Front's guerrillas. The mobilization of 1968 was a month later and trained. Nothing reached the generals, the soldier's family or the aid vote. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## Memo 010 — NCO education to the 2026 US standard for every US NCO and every RVNAF regular and territorial NCO from 1957, each course a gate for the next promotion

Memorandum 010 schooled every sergeant of both armies for his grade from 1957, the Americans in their services' 2026 courses and the ARVN and its territorials at the academy at Dong De, each course a gate for the next stripe. It completed what 007 and 009 began: from 1964 the Republic's squads and platoons were led by men taught the job, and when the field commissions emptied a squad, a corporal who had passed the leader's course took it. At Hau My in November 1966 a company that lost its officers in two minutes held, and lost fourteen men instead of forty to sixty; in the mobilization of 1968 one new PF platoon in fifteen lacked a schooled leader, not one in three. The enemy declined what kept its routine, read the routine from the academy's own manuals, and took what did not keep it. The gate survived the palace's decree of 1970, the only merit rule that did. None of it reached the corps commanders or the soldiers' families. Saigon falls on 30 April 1975, at rung (a).

## CP02 — Checkpoint

Checkpoint CP02 reviewed memoranda 006–010, which improved the Republic's army from the private to the battalion commander, and its posts and factories. The war is better at its floor and unchanged at its ceiling. ARVN battalions broken in 1966–67 are two-fifths to a half fewer than history's, the posts of the held belt keep their routine and are passed by an enemy who reads their manuals, and the enemy moves his war to what no provision reached: the relief, the mine, the self-defence group. Nothing reached who commands the corps, the fire the Republic owns, or the soldier's pay and family, which decided 1975. Eleven historical events in Phases I and II were consolidated into four, and three coherence fixes were made in Phase II. Seventeen of nineteen chains resolved as their authors predicted. Rung (a) stands; Saigon falls on 30 April 1975.

## Memo 011 — American Political Tolerance Package: the Watergate break-in never happens, a quarter of the historical draftees serve as volunteers, and the My Lai massacre does not happen

Memorandum 011 changed the war from Washington. In this war the Watergate burglary never happened, a quarter of the draftees volunteered, and nobody was killed at Son My. The volunteers and the missing massacre quieted the draft and the courtrooms of 1966–71 without changing the public's verdict or any battle. The removal of Watergate did what ten theater provisions could not: it reached the level at which the war was lost. Case–Church passed anyway, and no bomber returned. But a President who did not resign got the Republic about $950 million for fiscal 1975 instead of $700 million, with fuel and aircraft, and after Phuoc Long he asked Congress for more. Thieu, holding that money and that promise, refused on 11–14 March 1975 to give anything up. The Highlands fell after a three-week siege at Pleiku, Hue was withdrawn on 18 April and Da Nang was held. With no double collapse in March, the Politburo put Saigon back to the dry season of 1976. The end state moves for the first time, from rung (a) to (b): a reprieve of about a year, with the Republic's fall expected between February and May 1976.

## Memo 012 — Combined US–RVN–ROK–Australian operations command; combined interagency task force against the VCI

Memorandum 012 gave the war a combined command and a finishing arm against the infrastructure, and the second mattered more. The combined command survived Khanh's coup by passing its orders through his office (EV012-1). It closed seams the enemy then stopped using, and made Hue one battle that ended five days early (EV000-44). Its transfer to Vietnamese command began in the Delta in 1966 and stopped at the palace's corps commanders (EV012-6), and an agent sat in its plans cell for two and a half years (EV012-7). The task force broke the Can Giuoc security section in 1964 and, in FOLLOW THROUGH, the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region's tax administration west of Saigon (EV012-2, EV012-4). At Tet the attackers crossed Hoc Mon with no one to guide them (EV012-8). On the coast its list killed a family and was abandoned (EV012-5). The end state does not move: rung (b), with the Republic's fall expected in 1976.
